Chapter Two: Naming the Invisible—Finding Words for Emotional Labor
Have you ever felt a strange sense of relief when you finally found the right word for something you’ve been feeling for years? It’s like flipping on a light in a dark room. That’s what happens for a lot of people when they learn about emotional labor. Suddenly, all that frustration and exhaustion makes sense. It’s not just about being busy or a little disorganized—it’s about the daily work of managing emotions, smoothing over conflicts, and anticipating everyone’s needs, all while making it look totally effortless.
Let’s look at a familiar scene. Imagine a partner, worn out, trying to explain why she feels so overwhelmed. She starts listing all the things she keeps track of: birthdays, appointments, making sure everyone’s comfortable and happy. Her partner listens, but doesn’t quite get it. He says, “Just ask for help,” not realizing that asking is another job on its own. The conversation ends, but both walk away feeling misunderstood. The gap between them? It just got a little wider.
And it’s not just at home. Think about the workplace. There’s always that one colleague—the one who remembers everyone’s birthdays, knows who likes which snacks, and steps in when tempers flare. She does it because she cares, but also because no one else steps up. If she tries to pull back, things fall apart, and she’s left feeling guilty, like she’s let everyone down.
Here’s the thing: most people don’t even notice this kind of work, because it’s supposed to be invisible. The whole point is to keep things running smoothly, to stop problems before they even start. But the cost? It’s huge. Over time, the person doing all this extra work starts to feel invisible, too. Their efforts get taken for granted, and their own needs keep getting pushed aside.
Naming emotional labor is really the first step toward making things better. When you can finally see the patterns in your own life—and realize you’re not alone—it’s a game changer. Suddenly, you can have conversations you never could before. You can say, “This is emotional labor, and it’s too much for one person.” That makes it possible to ask for help, set some boundaries, and actually share the load.
Of course, just having a name for it doesn’t mean the problem disappears overnight. There’s still pushback, from others and even from ourselves. A lot of us grew up believing that caring for everyone else is just what it means to be a good partner, parent, or friend. It can feel selfish to ask for help, or to say no. And there’s always that fear—what if people see you as difficult, or demanding? So, you stay quiet, even when you’re completely overwhelmed.
Still, having the words gives you power. You start to notice when the balance is off, and it gets a little easier to speak up when something feels unfair. With time, small changes start to build. Maybe a partner notices when you’re running on empty. Maybe a coworker steps in to help with the organizing. The work is still there, but it’s not invisible anymore—and that alone can make all the difference.
